paragraphs.source_en: Possible practical reasons for the pottery decoration cannot be excluded, such as roughening the surface of a container by impressing or puncturing, to facilitate handling of heavy vessels when hot or wet (Rice 1999). But such an explanation does not seem to be the main reason for the decoration in the Central Sahara because the range of motifs here is limited and repetitive. There is no experimentation in the incised or punctured motifs but, on the contrary, all decorations are very conservative. Here, a striking similarity can be observed between the pottery decoration and the Round Head paintings, namely their strong conservatism and homogeneity throughout a vast area. Can a closer relationship between the pottery and the Round Head paintings be observed?

paragraphs.source_en: In the first published book about Round Heads, Sansoni (1994) believes that some body decoration motifs, especially the female ones, resemble the decoration of the earliest Central Saharan pottery, mainly the wavy line and dotted wavy line motifs. This idea was later expanded by Barich (1998b) arguing that the mastery of ceramic technology eventually attributed a great status to women because they were closely linked to pots, so much as to be identified with them and this would also appear in the Round Head art. It is not by chance that the female figures are sometimes richly decorated with motives typical of the ceramic repertoire and it would testify the importance given to the woman (Barich 1998b).
